draft.title: Why we sand between coats
draft.meta_description: A seamless finish starts between the coats: why we scuff every coat at 320 grit, what skipping it costs a contractor, and the 41-door job that proves it.
draft.excerpt: The step most shops skip when the schedule slips is the step that decides whether the finish is still on the door at month eighteen.

sources.claim: keyed coats hold the cross-hatch adhesion test where unkeyed coats flake
the pass adds about twenty minutes a door

draft.body_markdown:
We sand between coats on every door because it is the step that decides whether the finish is still on the door at month eighteen. Most shops skip it when the schedule slips. Here is what the pass does, what skipping it costs, and the job that proves it.

## What the second coat needs from the first

A coat of lacquer cures to a hard, closed surface. The next coat can sit on it, but it cannot grip it. A light pass with 320-grit paper opens that surface into thousands of tiny scratches - the key - and the next coat flows into them and locks. Without the key, the coats are two layers resting on each other. They look fine on install day. They part at the first hard knock, usually at the seams of a door frame, and the finish lifts.

## What skipping it costs

A lifted finish does not stay the shop's problem. It lands on the contractor's invoice as a call-back, and we have written up [what a call-back actually costs a two-crew contractor](https://brightsidefixtures.example/blog/what-a-call-back-costs): the day, the crew, and the client who does not book the next kitchen.

## How we run it

Our [finish schedule](https://brightsidefixtures.example/blog/finish-schedule) has the scuff pass between every coat, not just before the top coat. The paper is 320, the pass is light, and the dust is wiped before the next coat goes on. It adds about twenty minutes a door. Adhesion testing on keyed against unkeyed coats is well documented: the [cross-hatch results](https://finishing-standards.example/adhesion/cross-hatch) show the keyed coat holding where the unkeyed one flakes.

## The job that proves it

Harlow Street was 41 doors for a repeat trade client, delivered in June 2025 with the scuff pass between every coat, and the numbers are in the [finish schedule](https://brightsidefixtures.example/blog/finish-schedule) write-up. At the 18-month check none of the 41 had lifted, and the contractor had not scheduled a call-back week. That is the whole argument: the finish looked the same at month eighteen as it did on install day.

## What to ask your shop

Do not ask how many coats. Ask what happens between them. A shop that answers "we sand" without a grit and a pass is guessing. A shop that answers "320, light, every coat" has a schedule you can hold it to. Book a showroom visit and we will show you ours.
